A complete metabolic panel showed acute kidney injury with creatinine 2.3 mg/dL (reference range: 0.5-1.4 mg/dl), no coagulopathy, elevated venous lactate of 6.3 with a normal anion gap, and inflammatory markers were mildly elevated including procalcitonin 1.31 ng/mL, D-dimer 3.32 mcg/mL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 24 mm/hour and C-reactive protein (CRP) 5.9 mg/dL.

report.source_text: He was treated with high dose IV methyl prednisone for PAN, after infection was ruled out. Due to the severity, therapy with IV cyclophosphamide therapy 15 mg/kg once every two weeks for three doses was initiated, followed by 15 mg/kg once every three weeks for three to six months, in combination with a glucocorticoid taper with prednisone.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 48-year-old male with polysubstance use presented with insidious onset generalized abdominal pain and nausea. Initial labs revealed acute kidney injury with elevated creatinine (2.3 mg/dL), normocytic normochromic anemia, and mildly elevated inflammatory markers. Imaging demonstrated a 2 cm lobulated saccular aneurysm in the left gastric or splenic artery with hemoperitoneum due to aneurysmal rupture. ANCA serologies were negative, and hepatitis B and C serologies were negative, excluding secondary causes. The patient was treated with high dose IV methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide after infection exclusion. IR-guided embolization of the splenic artery pseudoaneurysm was performed with cessation of bleeding. No histopathology or biopsy was available. The diagnosis of PAN was supported by imaging, clinical and laboratory findings, and therapeutic response despite not fulfilling ACR criteria.
